item.content:encoded:
Good morning! Last night, Chad Tracy gave at-bats to two pinch-hitters in the 8th inning: lefty killer Jahmai Jones and utility infielder Andruw Monasterio. Jones did his job in the 8th, singling to start the inning in place of Mickey Gasper, but would subsequently strike out to end the game in the 9th. Jones was a platoon revelation when he first arrived in Boston, but he's cooled off since then (a .200 batting average over his last 12 games), and his positional inflexibility makes him a difficult roster fit. Monasterio did not do his job last night. He struck out with the bases loaded, putting an end to the biggest threat the Sox had all night.
In light of last night's events it's time to ask: Is it time for Romy Gonzalez to get another crack? Romy theoretically combines the best of both Jones and Monasterio — he's a lefty-killer and a utility infielder. He struggled mightily in his (rushed) return to the Sox earlier this year and has recently been battling a nagging injury lately, but his AAA line reads .344/.400/.505 with 3 homers and 6 doubles. He could inject some pop just as the Sox look like they could use a little extra juice.
Use this space to talk about bench bats and whatever else you want, and, as always, be good to one another.

item.content:encoded:
BOSTON — In a one-run game against the Kansas City Royals’ last homestand, Boston Red Sox shortstop Trevor Story hit a one-out double off the wall, raced to second base and dove head-first into the bag.
He flipped over on his back and held onto the bag, a safe call upheld after a Royals’ challenge.
Advertisement
The Red Sox eventually lost that game, but it was a small play that represented the bigger picture: Story was back. A diving, flipping play would have been hard to imagine for Story — or anyone watching him — earlier this season as he battled through a sports hernia injury that left him hitting .206 with a .547 OPS after 41 games.
Following surgery in May and a rehab that forced him to miss 93 games this season, Story has made a quiet but impactful return to the team.
He has hit safely in 13 of 14 games since returning, including Tuesday’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers. Since his activation Aug. 30 in New York, Story has started at shortstop in 14 of the team’s 15 games, going 19-for-56 (.339) with seven doubles and six RBIs. He’s hoping to make up for lost time.
“That was, ideally, the point of the surgery, to get it and come back and be able to do the things that I know I can do,” the 33-year-old said.
“It’s not invisible,” he said of the sports hernia’s effects. “I don’t think you would expect it to be after surgery and coming back. But it’s so much better than it was, and I’m getting stronger. So I’m happy about that. And I’m happy with the way my body has reacted. I wanted to be a part of this.”
It’s admittedly a small sample size since Story has returned, but if he had started slowly following his return, the calls for him to be replaced in the lineup would have grown louder. His replacements at shortstop — particularly a combination of Andruw Monasterio and Nick Sogard — filled in admirably during his absence as the Red Sox turned their season around. Story’s unproductive 10 rehab games with Triple-A Worcester, coupled with the rise of top prospect Franklin Arias, a shortstop raking at Triple A, created an echo chamber of angst about Story returning and underperforming.
So far, he hasn’t.
Advertisement
And he’s heard much of the criticism and frustration about his impending return. He understands it. His injury-riddled tenure in Boston has warranted that consternation. He missed much of 2024 recovering from extensive shoulder surgery and 2023 from elbow surgery. Of his five years in Boston, on a six-year, $140 million deal, he’s played only one healthy season.
Staying on the field has been his biggest bugaboo with the Red Sox. But the outside noise and frustration with his injuries motivated Story to prove he can still play.
“You see a lot of that stuff, but I really try to channel it into an energy in a way that I can use,” he said. “At the time, I wasn’t trying to pay much attention to it, but people would bring it to me, and I decided how I was going to look at it. I just tried to channel it into when I do come back, and it’s all about the playoffs, and it’s all about winning this thing at the end. That’s where I put my energy and focus.”
Roman Anthony, who missed 101 games with a torn finger ligament and rehabbed alongside Story, learned by watching the veteran handle the pressure.
“He’s unbelievable,” said Anthony. “Getting to go through this process with him. I was so happy for him. Every at-bat, he just continues to look better and better, and then to trust himself through all the noise.”
The return to the field has taken Story some effort, though. He arrives at the field roughly an hour before the team’s mandatory report time so that he can get on the trainer’s table to be stretched out for 30 to 45 minutes before his activation work in the gym, which leads into the team’s daily hitters’ meeting, then his workout before cage and field work.
“I’ve learned to kind of streamline it a little bit, and with the injury, (I) kind of know what (I) need,” he said. “In the gym, I’m just activating the right muscles, getting the core going, getting the hips right, adductor, glute med, the surrounding muscles from my surgery. So a lot of it is pre-hab. It’s mainly about the hips and getting the rotations right.”
Advertisement
The work has paid off early on. On Aug. 31, his first game back at Fenway Park in nearly four months, he cranked a base hit off the wall in the bottom of the ninth for a walk-off win.
This past Sunday, he padded a slim Red Sox lead against the Royals with a two-run single in the eighth. He’s hoping to carry this production through the rest of the season to prove he can be the player who hit .289 with an .827 OPS over the final four months of the 2025 season.
Despite missing so much of the year, the recent production since has helped him feel a part of the Red Sox’ run.
“As I’m sitting there watching the 15-game winning streak and starting to turn the whole season around, you watch it from the dugout and it’s like, ‘Man, this is something special,'” he said. “To be able to play a part and do my thing this late in the season means a lot to me.”

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — For the Red Sox, the vision of contention in 2026 seemed straightforward.
The team’s championship window had been pried open by the presence of a pair of cornerstones, with Garrett Crochet anchoring the rotation and Roman Anthony representing a lineup anchor not only for this year but several seasons to come.
But while the Sox are amid a magic-number countdown to a playoff berth, they’ve done so without Anthony and Crochet for most of the year. Their season has been saved in no small part by players who have emerged from obscurity to play critical roles — with essential contributions coming from Andruw Monasterio, Anthony Seigler, Mickey Gasper, Tsung-Che Cheng, Jahmai Jones, Tyron Guerrero, and more.
“I don’t think anybody had that on the drawing board,” said interim manager Chad Tracy with a chuckle. “They were asked to play a lot, and they produced. And if they didn’t, we were in trouble. It’s a huge piece of the 2026 season, no question.”
Of course, while no one expected the outsized impact of players who began the year as big league backups or in Triple-A, the Sox also took considerable pains to build organizational depth through a variety of transactions.
Whether it was an expanded version of the trade that brought Caleb Durbin from Milwaukee to include Monasterio and Seigler, or waiver claims of Cheng and Gasper, or a minor league deal for Guerrero, the season has been a case study in the notion that perceived little moves can have a huge impact.
“Every move and every decision matters,” said assistant general manager Mike Groopman, who oversees the team’s acquisitions group. “The big ones, whether it’s a larger free agent deal, [or] a larger, more high-profile trade, is naturally going to get a lot of attention.
“I don’t think this is unique to the Red Sox. There are 29 other teams that try to and do a very good job about caring about the ‘little’ things. But I think what we really try to reinforce is … that year over year, around the game, you see things that seem ‘little’ that end up being really impactful and big. [Deals that] seemed like small moves at the outset end up having a much, much larger impact commensurate with what would have been perceived at the time as a ‘larger’ move.”
Players who evolve from theoretical depth to become big league contributors excite numerous corners of an organization. The primary credit for those contributions, of course, belongs with a player, but they still often represent the combined efforts of personnel in scouting who identify the player’s potential contributions, player development personnel who help the player build on preexisting strengths and abilities in the minors, and big league staffers who help the players to perform at the game’s highest level.
Take Guerrero. After brief stints in the big leagues in 2018 and 2019, he’d become a journeyman, shuffling between organizations — and countries — but unable to forge a way back to the big leagues despite elite velocity.
But the Sox — who’d been interested in signing Guerrero before he pitched in the NPB in Japan in 2025 — remained intrigued, thanks in part to strong scouting recommendations from Kento Matsumoto in Japan and Manny Nanita in the Dominican Winter League. After they signed Guerrero to a minor league deal in the offseason, player development officials worked with him on some minor grip changes that unlocked significantly improved command with a sinker that regularly reached triple digits.
Guerrero’s dominance this year in Triple-A (0.92 ERA) essentially forced the Sox to call him up, and the 35-year-old emerged as a late-innings force from late June to late August (before shoulder fatigue led to a bad outing followed by a trip to the injured list), posting a 2.13 ERA over a 23-appearance stretch.
Again, the lion’s share of the credit goes to Guerrero for the work he did to fight his way back to the big leagues. But his emergence embodies the sort of under-the-radar acquisition that helped save the Sox’ season.
“The connection and integration between acquisition and development is really important,” said Groopman. “Guerrero and our [player development] group put a lot of time into [those changes] in the spring and the early season, to get him to a point where he was able to lock in some of these changes and unlock what was super obvious arm talent into something that was translating more consistently onto the major league mound.”
Of course, talent alone doesn’t dictate success once a depth player gets to the big leagues. They must also have the opportunity to contribute — and, in many cases, the freedom to fail while getting their bearings.
Tracy, who spent time with nearly all of this year’s depth contributors in Triple-A at the beginning of the year, has been mindful of creating an environment in which call-ups can contribute.
“I’m in the same boat [as them]. I want the freedom to go manage the game [as a first-time big league manager],” said Tracy. “I need to manage a game and feel like if I do something that doesn’t go right, it’s not the end of the world. If I feel that way, then I want the player to feel like, ‘Hey, if you go out there and play second base today and you make an error, move on to the next play.’
“If the culture becomes, ‘If I make a mistake, then all of a sudden I clam up and I get really tight,’ we’re going to have a problem. So you look at them and say, ‘You’re here for a reason: To go play your game. Don’t worry about making a mistake. Move on to the next pitch, next play.’ And they did that, and they were awesome.”
Alex Speier can be reached at alex.speier@globe.com. Follow him @alexspeier.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Patrick Sandoval allows four runs in second, Red Sox lose opener to Rangers

item.content:encoded:
Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. Entering Tuesday, the Red Sox left-hander had allowed a 6.12 ERA over his last five starts, but coming out of the gate Sandoval looked like he’d finally figured things out.
But after striking out the first four batters he faced, the wheels came off in the bottom of the second.
Sandoval allowed four runs over an interminable 44-pitch second inning and ultimately got the hook after recording just eight outs in Boston’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers.
Nick Sogard hit a two-run home run to help get the Red Sox back into the game, but the offense otherwise couldn’t get anything going against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers bullpen, squandering bases loaded opportunities in the fifth and eighth innings.
Sandoval started strong by striking out the side in the first inning, but after sending down Jake Burger to start the second everything ground to a screeching halt. The right-hander allowed a pair of singles, served up a two-run double to Elias Diaz, and then walked back-to-back batters to load the bases for five-time All-Star Corey Seager.
It appeared for a moment like Sandoval might minimize the damage when he drew a pop fly to shallow left, but the ball drifted into no-man’s land and Trevor Story couldn’t make the catch, allowing two more runs to score and putting the Rangers up 4-0.
Sandoval ultimately needed 44 pitches to get through the second, blowing up his pitch count and ensuring a long evening for the Red Sox bullpen. He recorded two outs in the third and was lifted for Brayan Bello after allowing four runs over 2 2/3 innings.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Arlington postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
Four runs matches the largest deficit the Red Sox have overcome in a win this season, but the club didn’t need long to cut it in half. After Caleb Durbin reached on a one-out single in the top of the third, Sogard ripped a line drive off deGrom that cleared the right field fence for a two-run home run.
It was the fifth home run of the season for Sogard, all of which have come since Aug. 19. Prior to that the 29-year-old had never hit a homer over his first three seasons as a big leaguer.
That wound up being as close as Boston got.
The Red Sox could have tied the score or taken the lead with one swing in the fifth inning, but despite loading the bases without recording a hit the club couldn’t get a run across. Jarren Duran was hit by a pitch, Durbin reached on catcher’s interference and Mickey Gasper walked to bring up Adley Rutschman with two outs, but the catcher grounded out to short to keep it a 4-2 game.
Boston’s bullpen did its part to keep the Red Sox in the game. Bello tossed 1 2/3 perfect innings, Alec Gamboa threw one scoreless aided in large part by a brilliant double play turned by Sogard to end the fifth, and Wyatt Olds worked his way out of a runners-at-the-corners, two-out jam to escape the sixth. Jovani Moran entered with a man on in the seventh and got three quick outs, setting the table for one last Red Sox push in the eighth.
Jahmai Jones sparked the rally with a leadoff single, Willson Contreras drew a one-out walk, and after Wilyer Abreu grounded out to move the two runners into scoring position Story was intentionally walked to load the bases again.
Rather than have Duran face the left-hander Jacob Latz, Tracy pinch hit Andruw Monasterio, but the move didn’t pay off. Monasterio worked a full count and nearly went deep on a hard hit liner that landed just foul before striking out to leave them loaded again.
Boston went quietly in the top of the ninth, finishing the game 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position while stranding nine men on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up and we couldn’t do it tonight,” Tracy said.
Magic number still 5
In addition to keeping pace in the AL West race, the Rangers also jumped the Toronto Blue Jays to become the first team below the AL Wild Card cutline. As a result the Red Sox’s magic number remains five despite the Blue Jays’ 10-1 loss earlier in the night.
Boston (82-69) can clinch a playoff berth as early as Friday, and depending on how things play out in the AL Central the Red Sox could lock down the second Wild Card spot as soon as this weekend.
Houck scoreless with WooSox
Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery rehab) tossed a scoreless inning of relief in his latest rehab appearance with the WooSox on Tuesday. The right-hander entered the game in the seventh inning and allowed one walk, no hits and struck out three over 22 pitches.

item.title: [FanGraphs] Checking in on the Cy Young Races

item.content:encoded:
Cam Schlittler brought his A-game on Sunday. Facing the Mets in the rubber game of the Subway Series at Yankee Stadium, the Yankees’ fireballer was nearly untouchable over the course of six scoreless innings, striking out eight while allowing just one hit, a fifth-inning double by Brett Baty. Meanwhile in Baltimore, the Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease worked around five walks to allow just one run over five innings while striking out nine. The two righties are engaged in an intriguing race for the AL Cy Young Award, one that could go down to the wire. The NL race is a tight one as well, with the Brewers’ Jacob Misiorowski the favorite but hardly the only one under consideration.
The 25-year-old Schlittler and 24-year-old Misiorowski are undeniably the frontrunners in their respective leagues, from both statistical and narrative standpoints. They lead in our Tom Tango-modeled Cy Young projections, and as of mid-August, they dominated polls taken by MLB.com. Nonetheless, the statistical races that can influence both our perceptions and voter behavior aren’t entirely decided, and with less than two weeks to go in the regular season, the races are worth a closer look.
The 6-foot-7 Misiorowski and 6-foot-6 Schlittler share similarities beyond their impressive heights. Both are in their first full major league seasons, after arriving in mid-2025 and helping their teams to the playoffs while showing poise beyond their years; this October, they’ll be seasoned postseason veterans. They’re the majors’ two hardest-throwing starters, with Misiorowski breaking velocity records all over the place. His average four-seam velocity — a mind-blowing 100.6 mph — not only leads the majors, but it’s also the fastest single-season velocity by a starter in the pitch-tracking era (from 2008 onward), hardly surprising given that he owns the (scrolling, scrolling, scrolling) 117 fastest pitches by a starter in pitch-tracking history — including a record-setting 105.5-mph heater to the Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 26 — and 353 of the 394 pitches of at least 102 mph thrown by a starter. Hunter Greene is the only other one in double digits (12). Schlittler merely ranks second among all starters this year, with an average velocity of 98.0 mph, which is still good for fifth in the pitch-tracking era.
Both righties have other exceptional offerings that test the adage “man cannot live by fastball alone,” in that Misiorowski’s cutter and Schlittler’s sinker are their second-most valuable pitches according to Statcast. But whatever they’re throwing, they’re dominating. Each leads his respective league in ERA (1.95 for both) and fWAR (6.0 for Misiorowski, 5.9 for Schlittler), with the Yankee additionally leading the AL in starts (31), innings (184 2/3), strikeout-walk differential (25.5%), and bWAR (7.1), and the Brewer leading the NL in strikeouts (236), strikeout rate (38.3%), and FIP (2.24). That ought to be enough to hand out the hardware, right?
Quite possibly, but not all of those statistical leads is insurmountable. Zooming in for a closer look first at the AL, Schlittler and Cease have separated themselves from the pack more so than they have from each other:
| Pitcher | W | L | GS | IP | K% | BB% | K-BB% | HR/9 | ERA | xERA | FIP | fWAR | bWAR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cam Schlittler | 14 | 6 | 31 | 184.2 | 31.6% | 6.1% | 25.5% | 0.78 | 1.95 | 2.88 | 2.57 | 5.9 | 7.1 |
| Dylan Cease | 11 | 5 | 28 | 166.1 | 35.3% | 10.8% | 24.6% | 0.60 | 2.38 | 2.81 | 2.48 | 5.6 | 6.0 |
| Parker Messick | 11 | 9 | 29 | 172.1 | 26.0% | 6.9% | 19.1% | 0.84 | 2.51 | 3.07 | 3.11 | 4.5 | 5.7 |
| Drew Rasmussen | 14 | 5 | 28 | 160.1 | 25.6% | 4.3% | 21.3% | 0.79 | 2.81 | 3.11 | 2.88 | 4.6 | 3.9 |
| Sonny Gray | 17 | 5 | 27 | 156.2 | 22.0% | 6.6% | 15.4% | 0.86 | 2.76 | 3.84 | 3.46 | 3.2 | 4.0 |
I couldn’t fit it in the table, but Schlittler is third in strikeouts (228) behind Cease (236) and Gavin Williams (235), whose run prevention numbers (3.78 ERA, 3.49 FIP) rule him out here. (Dan Szymborski has a closer look at Williams’ breakout up today.) Messick, Rasmussen, and Gray have all authored fine seasons, but none has a compelling enough statistical case to elevate him into the company of the top two; win totals and winning percentage don’t cut it these days. The ability of Schlittler and Cease to miss bats separates them in value from the rest of the group, both via our FIP-driven WAR and Baseball Reference’s version, where they don’t have to share as much credit (or blame) with their fielders given the lower rates of balls in play. More on that subject in a moment.
With Gerrit Cole scuffling late in his first season after returning from Tommy John surgery, and Max Fried limited to 18 starts by a bone bruise in his elbow, Schlittler has emerged as the Yankees’ bona fide ace and as one of the league’s true workhorses. Six other AL pitchers have made at least 30 starts so far, but only Michael Wacha has thrown at least 180 innings; he’s at 182 2/3, and while Tanner Bibee (177 1/3), Reid Detmers (174), Williams (174) and a couple others may get there, they won’t catch Schlittler. Nineteen of Schlittler’s starts have been quality starts, the league’s second-highest total behind Wacha (20); Cease is tied for eighth with 15. Schlittler has either put up zeroes or allowed just one run in 22 starts, including each of his last seven. Sixteen of those zero-or-one-run starts have lasted at least six innings; Gray and Rasmussen are among those tied for second with 13, while Cease is tied for sixth with 12. Beyond the aforementioned categories in which he’s led the league, Schlittler is second to Cease in FIP and xERA by less than one-tenth of a run, with the third-highest strikeout rate and sixth-lowest walk rate.
Cease, whom the Blue Jays signed to a seven-year, $210 million deal this past winter, has bounced back from an uneven 2025 performance with the Padres, one in which he put up a 4.54 ERA and a 3.56 FIP. He’s been every bit as good as the Blue Jays could have hoped for, something that can’t be said for many players on the defending AL champions. He has totaled seven starts of at least six innings with zero runs allowed, tied for third in the majors behind Cristopher Sánchez (10) and Rasmussen (eight); Schlittler is tied for seventh with six.
Cease has been the most unhittable starter in the AL, with the lowest batting average allowed (.177) and fewest hits per nine (5.68). He chalked up the first no-hitter of his career in 2024 while pitching for the Padres, and has flirted with a second one on a couple occasions this season. He tossed eight hitless innings on July 8 against the Giants at Oracle Park before allowing a single to Heliot Ramos to start the ninth, at which point he departed, having thrown 118 pitches in what was by then a 10-0 rout; days later, he was named to start the All-Star Game for the AL. He pitched 6 2/3 hitless innings against the Yankees on August 22 in the Bronx before allowing back-to-back singles to Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Austin Wells, and additionally threw a one-hit shutout against the Red Sox at Fenway Park on July 25, with a fifth-inning double by Andruw Monasterio the lone blemish.
Both Schlittler and Cease have averaged a hair under six innings per start (5.96 for the former, 5.94 for the latter). The difference in innings totals comes down to Cease’s having spent 15 days on the injured list for a mild hamstring strain starting in late May.
Cease has the higher strikeout rate, but also the higher walk rate — the highest among AL qualifiers, in fact — but even with that, his FIP and xERA are slightly better than Schlittler’s. Those estimators are defense-independent, but it’s worth noting the defenses behind the two pitchers. Statcast, which tracks the individual Fielding Run Values accumulated behind each pitcher, shows Cease with slightly more support, with his fielders putting up 7 FRV behind him compared to 5 FRV for Schlittler. The bWAR calculations, which start with actual runs allowed per nine innings with a variety of adjustments for defense, opposing offenses, and park factors, credit Cease with having the better defense behind him (based on team-level Defensive Runs Saved), worth 0.24 runs per nine to Schlittler’s 0.09 runs per nine. In other words, by that reckoning Cease shares more credit with his fielders, though that difference is canceled out by adjustments for his facing better offenses and pitching in a higher-scoring environment.
In the end, Schlittler’s combination of superior run prevention, better peripherals, and a larger innings load separates him from Cease by 1.1 bWAR and 0.3 fWAR. Depending upon where you fall on the spectrum of factoring in defense, it’s somewhere between a narrow margin and a substantial one, but either way it lines up with the consensus. Barring a blowup over his final couple of starts, Schlittler looks like the right call for the AL Cy Young.
The NL race isn’t as clear-cut:
| Pitcher | W | L | GS | IP | K% | BB% | K-BB% | HR/9 | ERA | xERA | FIP | fWAR | bWAR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jacob Misiorowski | 14 | 5 | 27 | 161.1 | 38.3% | 6.7% | 31.7% | 0.78 | 1.95 | 2.10 | 2.24 | 6.0 | 5.6 |
| Cristopher Sánchez | 17 | 5 | 30 | 187.1 | 27.0% | 5.4% | 21.6% | 0.77 | 2.79 | 3.31 | 2.72 | 5.8 | 7.6 |
| Chris Sale | 14 | 9 | 26 | 157.0 | 30.3% | 4.9% | 25.4% | 0.52 | 2.18 | 3.05 | 2.29 | 5.7 | 5.5 |
| Jesús Luzardo | 14 | 5 | 29 | 178.2 | 29.4% | 8.8% | 20.7% | 0.76 | 2.87 | 2.85 | 2.78 | 5.5 | 6.4 |
On a pure rate basis, the numbers favor Misiorowski. Not only does he lead the NL in the half-dozen categories highlighted above, but he’s been even more unhittable than Cease, with a .155 batting average allowed and 4.91 hits per nine given up, both tops in the majors among qualifiers. But because he’s worked in a six-man rotation all season long, and has been kept on a slightly shorter leash — averaging 5.97 innings per start to Sale’s 6.04, Luzardo’s 6.14, and Sánchez’s 6.24 — he has thrown 26 fewer innings than Sánchez.
The results have generally been dazzling. Misiorowski has 10 starts with double-digit strikeout totals, second in the majors only to Williams; Cease has nine, Luzardo six, Sánchez five, Sale and Schlittler four. The Miz has six scoreless starts of at least six innings, including a 15-strikeout one-hit shutout against the Phillies on June 12, marred only by a fourth-inning Kyle Schwarber single. But even with a majors-leading 236 strikeouts, the innings total puts him at a slight disadvantage in some contexts. Misiorowski is tied for fifth in the league with 18 quality starts, with Sánchez tied for second (20) alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto, one behind Sandy Alcantara; Sale is fourth with 19, Luzardo tied for ninth with 17. Misiorowski’s total of 11 starts of at least six innings with no more than one run allowed trails Sánchez (13), as well as Luzardo and Sale (12 apiece).
Sánchez has the volume advantage. Working with a sinker that averages “only” 95.0 mph — offset by one of the game’s best changeups — he’s reached the 200-strikeout plateau for the second consecutive season; his 212 ranks third behind Misiorowski and Luzado (221). His strikeout rate ranks seventh, his walk rate third, his strikeout-walk differential fourth, behind Misiorowski, Sale, and Luzardo in that order. He made a huge impression earlier this season by reeling off a streak of 50 2/3 scoreless innings in May, the longest ever by a lefty, and the fifth longest of all time; not since Orel Hershiser’s 59-inning streak in 1988 broke Don Drysdale’s record had anyone reached 50. That streak helped Sánchez land the honor of starting the All-Star Game for the NL, though Misiorowski’s workload — he was scheduled to start on the Sunday before the game, officially ruling him out for the honor, and then was scratched from that outing due to arm fatigue — played a part. Even then, Sánchez’s 2.62 ERA was a full run per nine higher than Misiorowski’s. On that note, Sánchez has a 3.15 ERA and a 3.46 FIP since the break, though by FIP (2.70 before, 2.77 after), he’s been basically the same pitcher, and even his xERAs (3.24 before, 3.46 after) are closer than his actual ones.
The 37-year-old Sale has thrown even fewer innings than Misiorowski because he’s been given some extra rest between starts. It’s a choice that’s paid off handsomely for the Braves and for the pitcher, who cracked 100 mph on a pitch on August 27, his fastest since 2018, and who has been positively brilliant in the second half, with a 2.14 ERA and a 1.41 FIP, the latter thanks to a combination of a 32.6% strikeout rate, a 2.7% walk rate, and 0.15 homers per nine.
According to Statcast, Sale has gotten the best defensive support of this quartet at 5 FRV, ahead of Sánchez (3), Misiorowski (0), and Luzardo (-3). That defense has helped to offset Sale’s having an xERA almost a run higher than the Miz. The two are on nearly even footing in the grand scheme, but based on their performances to date, I don’t see anything that would elevate Sale past Misiorowski except some sentiment for the old guy, a likely future Hall of Famer.
As for Luzardo, there’s not much separating him from Sánchez. Though his season hasn’t been as eye-catching, it’s been stellar, but in the wake of his two-hit, 12-strikeout shutout against the Braves on September 7, he’s dealt with shoulder stiffness and inflammation. Thanks to a clean MRI, he’s avoided the injured list so far, though he did have a turn skipped, and it wouldn’t be surprising if his workload between here and October is dialed down.
The two Phillies have had to survive playing in front of the team’s notoriously lousy defense. Sánchez has the highest BABIP among NL qualifiers (.335), 41 points ahead of the seventh-ranked Luzardo (.294) and 101 points ahead of Misiorowski (.234). Where Statcast tracks the individual FRVs behind each pitcher, Baseball Reference’s WAR adjustments are at the team level, which may be heavy-handed for pitchers who differ in groundball/fly ball orientation. Sanchez’s 58.2% groundball rate leads the league, while Luzardo’s 48.3% is seventh; both are more dependent upon the team’s shaky infield than its more middling (but still not good) outfield. In the bWAR calculations, there’s about half a run per nine difference between those two (-0.24 for Luzardo, -0.26 for Sánchez) and the other pair (0.24 for Misiorowski, 0.27 for Sale). The latter duo Phillies pair also gets favorable adjustments for pitching in tougher ballparks (which are tracked individually). The adjustments give the two Phillies the higher bWARs, with Sánchez having the edge.
I think the overall choice comes down to Sánchez’s advantage in volume versus Misiorowski’s edge in dominance, and for some voters or otherwise interested observers, that steers it into subjective and/or aesthetic territory. I can understand favoring the guy at the vanguard of extreme velocity — not just because of the raw velo, but also for what he’s done with it in terms of unhittability and sheer brilliance — but I can also appreciate the impulse to reward a throwback, particularly one working under the adverse conditions of being backed by Trea Turner (-16 DRS, -10 FRV) and Alec Bohm (-8 DRS, -5 FRV). Based on their numbers to this point, I’d vote Misiorowski, but I’d hardly blame anyone for choosing Sánchez. Nevertheless, I suspect his second-half fade has probably doomed him to another second-place finish.
Brooklyn-based Jay Jaffe is a senior writer for FanGraphs, the author of The Cooperstown Casebook (Thomas Dunne Books, 2017) and the creator of the JAWS (Jaffe WAR Score) metric for Hall of Fame analysis. He founded the Futility Infielder website (2001), was a columnist for Baseball Prospectus (2005-2012) and a contributing writer for Sports Illustrated (2012-2018). He has been a recurring guest on MLB Network and a member of the BBWAA since 2011, and a Hall of Fame voter since 2021. Follow him on BlueSky @jayjaffe.bsky.social.

item.content:encoded:
We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.
